mt: 'WORDCRAFT WRITERS WORKSHOP' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE WORKSHOP DATED 2022 AND COMPOSED AT ITS GRAIN; A 2026 BACKLASH AGAINST ITS WRITERS ADDED; HOW MUCH OF EACH STORY THE MODEL WROTE NOT CARRIED
d: THE WORKSHOP, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-01: 'The Wordcraft Writers Workshop was a 2022 research project by Google’s PAIR (People + AI Research) and Magenta teams that explored AI-augmented creative writing.' Overview and setup (the tool, its features, the cohort 'under non-disclosure agreements', the results); '2026 Literary Backlash' (the project 'resurfaced widely on social media (such as Bluesky)' in August 2026; the criticism that participants 'had lent credibility to AI models trained on copyrighted literary works without consent'; participants' responses). Eight cards: Google (two), Magenta, ActuIA, The Algorithmic Bridge, Engadget, Coralflavor, Mezha.
reading: The innocent reading first. Asked for the workshop, the Overview gives its year, teams, tool, cohort and results, then the controversy over it in 2026, from Google's pages and press coverage.
findings: THE WORKSHOP AT ITS GRAIN. Teams, tool, the thirteen writers and the eight weeks agree with the site ('The workshop cohort consisted of 13 professional writers, who were given 8 weeks to use Wordcraft'); the three writers named are on the home page's list of stories. 'rehashed cliches' and writer's block are on the learn page ('Many authors noted that generations tended to fall into clichés'). 'under non-disclosure agreements' is on no saved source; the paper's terms are consent to publication and compensation ('Participants were compensated for participating in the study').

THE YEAR. 'a 2022 research project'; the Engadget card, 'Participation In 2022 Google AI Study'; Mezha, 'Google's 2022 AI experiment'. The census row: 'no date for the workshop in the saved sources (the paper cites work of 2022)'.

THE BACKLASH OF 2026. 'In August 2026, the project resurfaced widely on social media (such as Bluesky) after being highlighted by author Lily Lachance.' Three of the eight cards are its coverage (Engadget, Coralflavor, Mezha). The census row, built 2026-11-01, gives the workshop as 'historical', 'a completed eight-week workshop', and records nothing of this reception; its reading cites only the writers' own fear of 'reputational harm' from plagiarized suggestions.

THE DIVISION OF TEXT NOT CARRIED. The paper records how far each story was generated: 'largely formed around generated text (AP, DH, JM, MT, AW)', 'the bulk of the story text was written by the authors themselves (KL, WT, NG)', one writer who 'siloed out specific sections' (RS); the site's notice says the writers 'have not authored these stories under any sort of explicit guidance or instruction'. The composition says the tool 'required heavy manual filtering' and does not say whose name each story stands under or how much of it the model wrote; the criticism it reports falls on the writers as participants.
analysis: The workshop composed at its grain and dated, with a reception the census row does not record. The paper's account of each writer's share of the text, the census row's ground for reading authorship as held by the named writer, is absent.
per_note: Google's PAIR and Magenta teams named; the researchers who conducted it not named; the site and press carded.

atoms.reference: Google's PAIR and Magenta teams; conducted by Andy Coenen and Ann Yuan (PAIR), Daphne Ippolito and Sehmon Burnam (Magenta).

evidence.record_quote: The Wordcraft Writers Workshop is a collaboration between Google's PAIR and Magenta teams, and 13 professional writers from a diverse set of creative writing backgrounds.

The Wordcraft Writers Workshop was conducted by Andy Coenen and Ann Yuan, research engineers on the PAIR team, Daphne Ippolito, a research scientist working with Magenta , and Sehmon Burnam, a product manager at Magenta .

atoms.reference: A collaboration of Google's PAIR and Magenta teams with 13 professional writers, who were given 8 weeks to use Wordcraft, a LaMDA-powered tool for writing stories with AI.

evidence.record_quote: The Wordcraft Writers Workshop is a collaboration between Google's PAIR and Magenta teams, and 13 professional writers from a diverse set of creative writing backgrounds.
The workshop cohort consisted of 13 professional writers, who were given 8 weeks to use Wordcraft.
Wordcraft is a tool built by researchers at Google PAIR for writing stories with AI. The application is powered by LaMDA

atoms.reference: Thirteen stories, each under its writer's name (Robin Sloan, Allison Parrish, Aaron Winslow and others), of 1,000-1,500 words, with a whitepaper drawn from the writers' journals and interviews.

evidence.record_quote: Participants were asked to write a story of 1,000-1,500 words using Wordcraft.
Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers
We also conducted two 45 minute interviews with each participant

atoms.reference: To explore the limits of co-writing with LaMDA and foster an honest and earnest conversation about technology and creativity.

evidence.record_quote: Together we explore the limits of co-writing with LaMDA and foster an honest and earnest conversation about the rapidly changing relationship between technology and creativity.

atoms.reference: No instructions to the writers on how to use the tool or how much generated text to keep; the stories not authored under explicit guidance; Google does not endorse them; participants consented to publication and were compensated.

evidence.record_quote: We explicitly didn't give writers any instructions regarding how they should use the tool or how much of their final story text should be directly generated by Wordcraft.
The writers featured here have used Wordcraft along with their own creative vision and have not authored these stories under any sort of explicit guidance or instruction.
Google does not endorse the content of any of the stories contained on this website.

Participants consented to their stories being published in a digital literary magazine of human-AI collaborative stories, and to the use of their feedback in the journals and interviews in this whitepaper. Participants were compensated for participating in the study.
